prompt: In the NASM OPT model, which phase emphasizes improving muscular endurance and stabilizing the kinetic chain?

options.text: Phase 1: Stabilization Endurance
Phase 3: Muscular Development (Hypertrophy)
Phase 4: Maximal Strength
Phase 5: Power

explanation: Phase 1 Stabilization Endurance builds muscular endurance, joint stability and neuromuscular efficiency with high reps, slow tempos and proprioceptive challenge before heavier loads are introduced.

distractorExplanations.b: Phase 3 targets muscle size with 6–12 reps at 75–85% 1RM; it comes after stabilization is established.
distractorExplanations.c: Phase 4 Maximal Strength uses 85–100% 1RM loads for peak force, not endurance and joint stability.
distractorExplanations.d: Phase 5 Power pairs heavy strength work with fast power moves and assumes stabilization is already built.

prompt: When a client drives up out of the bottom of a squat, which muscle is the primary agonist for hip extension?

options.text: Adductor longus
Gluteus maximus
Rectus femoris
Tensor fasciae latae

explanation: The gluteus maximus is the prime mover (agonist) for hip extension, as when rising from a squat or climbing stairs, with the hamstrings as synergists. Rectus femoris, TFL and adductor longus mainly flex or adduct the hip.

distractorExplanations.a: Adductor longus adducts the hip and assists flexion; the gluteus maximus is the prime mover for hip extension.
distractorExplanations.c: Rectus femoris crosses the hip anteriorly and flexes it (and extends the knee); it opposes hip extension.
distractorExplanations.d: Tensor fasciae latae flexes, abducts, and internally rotates the hip; it does not drive hip extension like the gluteus maximus.

prompt: A biceps curl, a front lunge and a squat all occur mainly in which plane of motion, the plane that divides the body into left and right halves?

Transverse plane
Sagittal plane
Scapular plane

distractorExplanations.b: The transverse plane divides upper from lower body and hosts rotational motions such as trunk twists.
distractorExplanations.d: The scapular plane is a functional arm-elevation angle about 30° forward of frontal, not a cardinal body plane.

prompt: The structure linking the calf muscles to the calcaneus is an example of which connective tissue, the type that attaches muscle to bone?

options.text: Ligament
Bursa
Meniscus
Tendon

distractorExplanations.b: A bursa is a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between tissues; it does not anchor muscle to bone.
distractorExplanations.c: A meniscus is a fibrocartilage pad that cushions and deepens joints such as the knee, not a muscle attachment.

prompt: Which structure is the smallest functional contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fiber?

options.text: Myofibril
Sarcomere
Motor unit
Fascicle

explanation: The sarcomere, the segment between two Z-lines where actin and myosin filaments overlap, is the functional unit of muscle; cross-bridge cycling inside sarcomeres shortens the fiber and produces force.

distractorExplanations.a: A myofibril is a chain of many sarcomeres in series; the sarcomere is the smallest contractile unit.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus the fibers it innervates, a neural control unit, not a structure within a fiber.
distractorExplanations.d: A fascicle is a bundle of whole muscle fibers, a much larger level of organization than the sarcomere.

prompt: According to the length–tension relationship, at what point does a muscle produce its greatest force?

options.text: When it is fully shortened with maximal filament overlap
When it is stretched well past resting length
Near resting length, with optimal actin–myosin overlap
When its antagonist is shortened and fully active

explanation: Force peaks near optimal sarcomere length (near resting length), where actin and myosin overlap optimally; too short or too long reduces cross-bridge capacity.

distractorExplanations.a: Excess overlap at full shortening crowds the filaments and reduces cross-bridges; more overlap is not more force.
distractorExplanations.b: Stretching far past resting length leaves too little actin–myosin overlap, so fewer cross-bridges form.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses length–tension with reciprocal inhibition; a tight antagonist actually alters length and reduces force.

prompt: A client performs a maximal 6–8 second sprint. Which energy system supplies most of the ATP?

options.text: Oxidative (aerobic) system
Beta-oxidation of fatty acids
Anaerobic glycolysis
ATP–PC (phosphagen) system

explanation: Maximal efforts of up to about 10 seconds are fueled mainly by stored ATP and creatine phosphate (the ATP–PC system), the fastest way to regenerate ATP; glycolysis dominates roughly 30 s to 2 min and oxidative pathways longer work.

distractorExplanations.a: The oxidative system dominates longer, lower-intensity work; it cannot supply ATP fast enough for a sprint.
distractorExplanations.b: Fatty acid oxidation is the slowest ATP pathway and fuels low-intensity, prolonged activity.
distractorExplanations.c: Anaerobic glycolysis becomes the main supplier after about 10 seconds, in efforts lasting up to about 2 minutes.

prompt: During the lifting phase of a dumbbell biceps curl, which role does the triceps brachii play?

options.text: Antagonist, opposing the elbow flexion
Synergist, assisting the biceps in elbow flexion
Agonist, producing the elbow flexion
Stabilizer, holding the wrist steady

explanation: The biceps brachii is the agonist for elbow flexion in a curl. The triceps brachii extends the elbow, so it is the antagonist: it opposes the action and must relax for smooth flexion, then controls the lowering.

distractorExplanations.b: Synergists such as the brachialis and brachioradialis assist elbow flexion; the triceps opposes it.
distractorExplanations.c: The biceps brachii is the agonist producing elbow flexion; the triceps extends the elbow instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Wrist stability comes from the forearm flexors and extensors; the triceps crosses the elbow and shoulder.

The global muscular system
The central nervous system's motor control
The passive ligamentous restraint system

prompt: Which bony landmark is the primary distal attachment (insertion) of the biceps brachii?

options.text: Coracoid process of the scapula
Olecranon process of the ulna
Radial tuberosity of the radius
Deltoid tuberosity of the humerus

prompt: During an overhead squat assessment, a client shows excessive forward lean of the torso. Which muscles are most likely overactive?

options.text: Soleus, gastrocnemius, and hip flexor complex
Latissimus dorsi, teres major, and pectoralis major
Adductor complex, TFL, and vastus lateralis
Gluteus maximus, erector spinae, and anterior tibialis

explanation: Excessive forward lean is linked to overactive calves (soleus, gastrocnemius) and the hip flexor complex, with underactive anterior tibialis, gluteus maximus and erector spinae; tight calves limit dorsiflexion so the trunk tips forward.

distractorExplanations.b: Overactive lats, teres major and pecs drive the arms-fall-forward compensation, not torso lean.
distractorExplanations.c: Overactive adductors, TFL and vastus lateralis are associated with the knees moving inward (valgus).
distractorExplanations.d: These muscles are typically underactive with forward lean; they need activation rather than inhibition.

prompt: Viewed from the front during an overhead squat, a client's feet turn out. Which muscles are probably overactive?

options.text: Anterior and posterior tibialis together with the medial gastrocnemius
Soleus / lateral gastrocnemius and/or biceps femoris (short head)
Hip flexor complex, latissimus dorsi, and erector spinae
Adductor complex, TFL, and vastus lateralis

explanation: Foot/ankle compensation patterns often involve lateral calf and biceps femoris overactivity, with underactive medial gastrocnemius, medial hamstrings, gracilis, sartorius, and popliteus.

distractorExplanations.a: Tibialis and medial gastrocnemius are typically underactive (not overactive) in foot-turn-out and flattening patterns.
distractorExplanations.c: Overactive hip flexors, lats, and erector spinae describe the low-back-arches compensation, not feet turning out.
distractorExplanations.d: Overactive adductors, TFL, and vastus lateralis are the knee valgus (knees move in) pattern.

prompt: A new client's resting heart rate is taken on three mornings before getting out of bed. What does this measurement mainly give the trainer?

options.text: An accurate prediction of the client's age-predicted maximal heart rate
A reliable substitute for taking the client's resting blood pressure
A cardiorespiratory baseline to track and use in heart rate formulas
A direct measurement of the client's maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max)

explanation: Resting heart rate is a simple baseline of cardiorespiratory fitness and recovery: it tends to fall as fitness improves and is an input to heart rate reserve formulas. It is best measured on waking and averaged over several days.

distractorExplanations.a: Maximal heart rate is estimated from age-based formulas or a max test; resting heart rate does not predict it.
distractorExplanations.b: Blood pressure is a separate vital sign measured with a cuff; a normal pulse says nothing about BP.
distractorExplanations.d: VO2max is measured in a lab or estimated from field tests; resting heart rate alone cannot measure it.

1RM back squat test
Overhead squat assessment

prompt: A client's knees cave inward during a squat. Which muscles are most commonly underactive?

Adductor complex and TFL
Hip flexors and erector spinae
Soleus and lateral gastrocnemius

distractorExplanations.d: Overactive soleus and lateral gastrocnemius are linked to feet turning out, and they are overactive, not underactive.

explanation: Henneman's size principle: motor units are recruited from smallest (low-threshold, slow-twitch) to largest (high-threshold, fast-twitch) as force demand rises, so heavy loads recruit nearly all units while light sets use mainly small ones.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the size principle; large fast-twitch units are recruited last, when force demands are high.
distractorExplanations.b: Motor units are recruited progressively as force demand rises; they are not all active at light loads.
distractorExplanations.d: Slow, low-threshold units stay active at heavy loads; fast units are added on top, not substituted.

prompt: Late in a long fasted run, a client's blood glucose starts to fall. Which pancreatic hormone acts to raise it?

options.text: Glucagon
Insulin
Cortisol
Testosterone

explanation: Glucagon, released by pancreatic alpha cells when blood glucose falls, stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. Insulin, from beta cells, has the opposite effect after meals.

distractorExplanations.b: Insulin lowers blood glucose by moving it into cells; its release falls, not rises, as glucose drops.
distractorExplanations.c: Cortisol does help raise glucose over time, but it comes from the adrenal cortex, not the pancreas.
distractorExplanations.d: Testosterone is an anabolic sex hormone from the gonads with no direct role in restoring blood glucose.

prompt: Which type of synovial joint, found at the hip and shoulder, allows movement in all three planes of motion?

options.text: Modified hinge joint
Pivot (trochoid) joint
Saddle (sellar) joint
Ball-and-socket joint

explanation: Ball-and-socket joints, like the hip and glenohumeral joint, let a rounded head move within a cup, allowing flexion/extension, abduction/adduction and rotation across the sagittal, frontal and transverse planes.

distractorExplanations.a: Hinge joints such as the elbow mainly allow flexion and extension in a single (sagittal) plane.
distractorExplanations.b: Pivot joints such as the proximal radioulnar joint allow rotation around one axis, not motion in every plane.
distractorExplanations.c: Saddle joints such as the thumb's carpometacarpal joint move in two planes but do not rotate freely.

prompt: In a dumbbell curl, the biceps pulls on the forearm between the elbow (axis) and the weight in the hand. Which lever class is this, the most common in the body?

options.text: First-class lever
Second-class lever
Third-class lever
Wheel-and-axle system

explanation: In a third-class lever the effort (biceps insertion on the radius) lies between the axis (elbow) and the load (the dumbbell). Most limb joints work this way, trading mechanical advantage for speed and range of motion.

distractorExplanations.a: In a first-class lever the axis sits between force and load, as when the head nods on the atlas.
distractorExplanations.b: In a second-class lever the load sits between axis and force, as in a calf raise onto the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Wheel-and-axle describes rotating structures such as the trunk in rotation; the curl is a lever, not a wheel.

prompt: A desk-bound client breathes shallowly, with the shoulders rising on each breath. Which change in muscle use does this pattern reflect?

options.text: The diaphragm overworking while the scalenes switch off
Scalenes and other accessory muscles doing the diaphragm's work
The rectus abdominis taking over as the body's main inspiratory muscle
The intercostals stopping so the lungs fill passively

explanation: The diaphragm is the primary inspiratory muscle. With chronic shallow chest breathing, accessory muscles (scalenes, sternocleidomastoid, upper trapezius, pectoralis minor) overwork, which can feed upper-body postural problems such as forward head.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the pattern; shoulder-rising breaths show accessory muscles compensating for an underused diaphragm.
distractorExplanations.c: The rectus abdominis assists forced exhalation; it is not an inspiratory muscle.
distractorExplanations.d: The lungs cannot fill passively during inhalation; inspiratory muscles must expand the chest.

prompt: A trainer asks a client to complete as many push-ups as possible in 60 seconds. What does this test primarily measure?

options.text: Upper-body maximal strength
Upper-body explosive power
Upper-body muscular endurance
Shoulder flexibility and mobility

explanation: Repeating a bodyweight movement to fatigue within a time limit measures muscular endurance, the ability to produce repeated submaximal contractions. NASM's push-up test counts the reps completed in 60 seconds.

distractorExplanations.a: Maximal strength is tested with a heavy 1–5 rep load such as a bench press, not repeated bodyweight reps.
distractorExplanations.b: Power needs fast, explosive movement such as a medicine ball throw; steady push-ups to fatigue measure endurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Shoulder mobility is checked with range-of-motion tests; push-ups to fatigue show how long muscles keep working.

prompt: During an overhead squat assessment, which checkpoints does the trainer observe from the side (lateral) view?

options.text: Lumbo-pelvic-hip complex, shoulders, and head/cervical spine
Feet and knees, checking whether they turn out or move inward
Wrists and elbows, checking grip width and elbow flare
Knees and hips, checking for an asymmetric weight shift

explanation: From the anterior view the trainer watches the feet and knees; from the lateral view the LPHC (forward lean, low back arching), shoulders (arms falling forward) and head. Viewing both angles captures sagittal and frontal compensations.

distractorExplanations.b: Feet and knees are observed from the front (anterior) view, where turn-out and valgus are visible.
distractorExplanations.c: Wrists and elbows are not formal overhead squat checkpoints; arm position is judged at the shoulder.
distractorExplanations.d: Asymmetric weight shift is judged from the front or back, not from the side view.

prompt: A client's static posture shows flattened arches, knees angled inward, and internally rotated femurs. Which distortion pattern best fits?

options.text: Upper crossed syndrome
Lower crossed syndrome
Posterior pelvic tilt (swayback) pattern
Pronation distortion syndrome

explanation: Pronation distortion syndrome is characterized by foot pronation (flat feet) and knee valgus with tibial and femoral internal rotation and adduction. It is linked to tight peroneals and calves and weak posterior tibialis and gluteus medius.

distractorExplanations.a: Upper crossed syndrome involves rounded shoulders and a forward head, not the foot, knee and hip findings.
distractorExplanations.b: Lower crossed syndrome centers on anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis rather than flat feet and valgus.
distractorExplanations.c: Swayback shows the pelvis shifted forward with a posterior tilt; it does not explain collapsed arches and valgus.

prompt: During a standing cable row assessment, a client's head juts forward on each rep. Which muscles are most likely underactive?

options.text: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae
Deep cervical flexors
Sternocleidomastoid and scalenes
Latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major

explanation: A forward head during pulling or pushing suggests underactive deep cervical flexors with overactive upper trapezius, sternocleidomastoid and levator scapulae. Correctives lengthen the overactive neck muscles and activate chin-tuck strength.

distractorExplanations.a: Upper trapezius and levator scapulae are typically overactive in this pattern and need inhibiting, not activating.
distractorExplanations.c: The sternocleidomastoid and scalenes tend to be overactive when the head juts forward, not underactive.
distractorExplanations.d: Overactive lats and pecs go with the arms falling forward; they are not the weak link in a forward head.

prompt: Using the formula 208 − (0.7 × age), what is the estimated maximal heart rate for a 50-year-old client?

options.text: 158 bpm
170 bpm
173 bpm
178 bpm

explanation: Estimated HRmax = 208 − (0.7 × age) = 208 − (0.7 × 50) = 208 − 35 = 173 bpm. NASM uses this Tanaka-style formula; it is an estimate, and individuals can differ from it by 10 or more beats.

distractorExplanations.a: Subtracts the full age (208 − 50); the formula subtracts only 0.7 × age, which is 35.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the older 220 − age estimate; the formula given is 208 − (0.7 × 50) = 173.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses 0.6 instead of 0.7 (208 − 30); the correct step is 0.7 × 50 = 35, so 208 − 35.

prompt: A client has an estimated maximal heart rate of 180 bpm and a resting heart rate of 60 bpm. Using the heart rate reserve (Karvonen) method, what is the target heart rate at 70% intensity?

options.text: 84 bpm
126 bpm
144 bpm
186 bpm

explanation: Karvonen: THR = (HRmax − RHR) × intensity + RHR = (180 − 60) × 0.70 + 60 = 120 × 0.70 + 60 = 84 + 60 = 144 bpm. Using the reserve accounts for the client's resting heart rate.

distractorExplanations.a: Calculates 70% of the reserve (84) but forgets to add the resting heart rate back on.
distractorExplanations.b: Takes 70% of maximal heart rate (180 × 0.7); the Karvonen method works from heart rate reserve.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds resting heart rate to 70% of maximal heart rate; the reserve (180 − 60) must be used first.

prompt: NASM's Durnin–Womersley skinfold method uses which four sites?

options.text: Chest, abdomen, thigh, triceps
Waist, hips, neck, upper arm
Biceps, triceps, subscapular, iliac crest
Triceps, midaxillary, chest, medial calf

explanation: The Durnin–Womersley formula sums skinfolds at the biceps, triceps, subscapular and iliac crest (suprailiac) sites on the right side, then converts the total to body fat percentage using age- and sex-specific tables.

distractorExplanations.a: Chest, abdomen and thigh are Jackson–Pollock sites; Durnin–Womersley uses four upper-body and trunk sites.
distractorExplanations.b: Waist, hips, neck and arm are tape circumference sites, not skinfold caliper sites.
distractorExplanations.d: Midaxillary, chest and calf belong to other skinfold protocols, not the four-site Durnin–Womersley test.

prompt: Two clients have the same BMI, but one has a much higher waist-to-hip ratio. What does the higher ratio most suggest?

options.text: More abdominal (visceral) fat and higher cardiometabolic risk
Greater lower-body muscle mass and therefore lower health risk
A higher total body fat percentage than the other client
A larger frame size that needs a different BMI cutoff

explanation: Waist-to-hip ratio (waist ÷ hip circumference) shows where fat is stored. A higher ratio reflects more central, often visceral, fat, which is linked to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes independently of BMI.

distractorExplanations.b: A higher ratio means the waist is large relative to the hips, pointing to central fat rather than leg muscle.
distractorExplanations.c: Waist-to-hip ratio describes where fat is stored, not total body fat percentage.
distractorExplanations.d: Frame size is not judged from waist-to-hip ratio, and BMI cutoffs do not change with it.

prompt: A client's resting blood pressure averages 134/86 mm Hg over two visits. Under the ACC/AHA blood pressure categories, how is this classified?

options.text: Normal
Elevated
Stage 1 hypertension
Stage 2 hypertension

explanation: Under the ACC/AHA categories, stage 1 hypertension is systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 mm Hg. A reading of 134/86 meets both stage 1 ranges, so the trainer documents it and follows referral and medical-clearance policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Normal is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic; both readings here are higher.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevated is 120–129 systolic with diastolic under 80; a diastolic of 86 rules this out.
distractorExplanations.d: Stage 2 starts at 140 systolic or 90 diastolic; 134/86 is below both cutoffs.

prompt: Which piece of intake information is objective rather than subjective?

options.text: The client's description of daily stress
The client's report of past knee surgery
The client's stated goal of losing 10 lb
A measured resting heart rate of 68 bpm

explanation: Objective information is measurable and observable, such as heart rate, blood pressure, body composition and movement assessments. Subjective information comes from the client, including medical history, lifestyle, occupation and goals.

distractorExplanations.a: Self-reported stress is subjective information from a lifestyle questionnaire, not a measurement.
distractorExplanations.b: Medical history the client reports is subjective, even when it is important for screening.
distractorExplanations.c: Goals are subjective information collected through interview, not measured data.

prompt: A client takes a beta-blocker for hypertension. How should the trainer monitor cardio intensity?

options.text: Use age-predicted HR zones, since the drug does not affect heart rate
Use RPE or the talk test, since heart rate response is blunted
Raise HR targets by 20 beats to offset the medication
Avoid cardio entirely until the medication is stopped

explanation: Beta-blockers reduce resting and maximal heart rate and blunt the heart rate response to exercise, so HR-based zones are unreliable. RPE scales or the talk test give a safer gauge of intensity, alongside physician guidance.

distractorExplanations.a: Beta-blockers lower resting and exercise heart rate, so standard HR zones overestimate effort.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no fixed correction; the blunting varies, so perceived exertion replaces HR targets.
distractorExplanations.d: Clients on beta-blockers can do cardio with clearance; the change is in how intensity is monitored.

prompt: A client sits most of the workday and often wears high-heeled shoes. Which muscles are most likely shortened?

options.text: Hamstrings and anterior tibialis
Gluteus maximus and erector spinae
Hip flexors and calf muscles
Adductors and lower trapezius

explanation: Prolonged sitting holds the hips flexed, shortening the hip flexor complex, while high heels keep the ankle plantarflexed, shortening the gastrocnemius and soleus. Occupational questions help predict compensations seen in assessments.

distractorExplanations.a: Sitting shortens the hip flexors, not the hamstrings, and heels shorten the calves, not the shin muscles.
distractorExplanations.b: Prolonged sitting tends to leave the gluteus maximus lengthened and underactive, not shortened.
distractorExplanations.d: Neither sitting nor high heels systematically shortens the adductors or the lower trapezius.

prompt: Which assessment most directly measures a client's lower-body power?

options.text: Vertical jump test
Bodyweight squats to failure
YMCA 3-minute step test
Single-leg squat assessment

explanation: Power is force × velocity, so it is tested with maximal, explosive efforts such as the vertical jump or long jump, which show how fast the legs can produce force. Endurance and movement screens measure other qualities.

distractorExplanations.b: Squats to failure measure lower-body muscular endurance; power requires maximal effort over a short time.
distractorExplanations.c: The step test estimates cardiorespiratory fitness from recovery heart rate, not lower-body power.
distractorExplanations.d: The single-leg squat observes knee and hip control on one limb; it does not quantify explosive force.

prompt: A trainer counts 18 radial pulse beats in 15 seconds while the client rests. What is the client's resting heart rate?

options.text: 36 bpm
54 bpm
72 bpm
90 bpm

explanation: A 15-second count is multiplied by 4 to give beats per minute: 18 × 4 = 72 bpm. Counting a full 60 seconds, or averaging several mornings, improves accuracy for a resting value.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies by 2, which converts a 30-second count; a 15-second count is multiplied by 4.
distractorExplanations.b: Multiplies by 3, which would convert a 20-second count; a 15-second count needs × 4.
distractorExplanations.d: Multiplies by 5, which converts a 12-second count; the correct math is 18 × 4 = 72.

prompt: A client gets a bioelectrical impedance (BIA) body fat reading right after a sweaty workout without drinking. How is the reading likely affected?

options.text: Dehydration tends to underestimate body fat percentage
Hydration has no effect, because BIA measures fat directly
The reading changes only if the client ate a large meal
Dehydration tends to overestimate body fat percentage

explanation: BIA sends a small current through the body; water-rich lean tissue conducts well and fat conducts poorly. Dehydration raises impedance, so the device overestimates fat. Standardize hydration, meals and exercise timing before testing.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the effect: less body water raises impedance, which the device reads as more fat.
distractorExplanations.b: BIA estimates fat from electrical resistance through body water, so hydration strongly affects it.
distractorExplanations.c: Meals matter, but fluid lost through sweat also alters impedance and skews the estimate.

prompt: Which superset best fits OPT Phase 2 (Strength Endurance)?

options.text: Barbell bench press followed by a medicine ball chest pass
Barbell bench press followed by a stability ball push-up
Barbell bench press followed by an incline dumbbell press
Barbell bench press done as one heavy set of 3 reps

explanation: Phase 2 Strength Endurance supersets a more stable strength exercise with a less stable exercise of a similar movement pattern, such as a bench press then a stability ball push-up, for 8–12 reps each, building strength and stabilization together.

distractorExplanations.a: A strength move paired with an explosive throw is the Phase 5 Power superset, not Strength Endurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Two stable strength exercises for the same muscle is a hypertrophy-style pairing, not the Phase 2 superset.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavy low-rep sets with long rest are Phase 4 Maximal Strength; Phase 2 pairs strength with stability.

prompt: A 70 kg client in Phase 5 performs medicine ball chest passes. Using NASM's guideline for power-exercise load, what is the heaviest ball generally appropriate?

options.text: About 3.5 kg
About 7 kg
About 14 kg
About 21 kg

explanation: NASM sets power-exercise loads at about 30–45% 1RM for lifts, or up to about 10% of body weight for medicine balls, so the implement can be moved at maximal velocity. 10% of 70 kg = 7 kg.

distractorExplanations.a: 3.5 kg is 5% of body weight, within the guideline but not its upper limit of about 10%.
distractorExplanations.c: 14 kg is about 20% of body weight, too heavy to move explosively; the guideline caps near 10%.
distractorExplanations.d: 21 kg is 30% of body weight, a load that slows the throw so it no longer trains power.

prompt: A deconditioned new client starts cardiorespiratory training in Stage 1. Which intensity is most appropriate?

options.text: Zone 2, about 76–85% of HRmax, speech becoming difficult
Zone 3, about 86–95% of HRmax, in short hard intervals
Zone 1, about 65–75% of HRmax, able to hold a conversation
Alternating Zones 1 and 3 in equal one-minute bouts

explanation: Stage 1 builds an aerobic base in Zone 1 (about 65–75% of estimated HRmax, RPE about 3–4, talk test passed). Stage 2 adds Zone 2 intervals and Stage 3 adds Zone 3 intervals as fitness improves.

distractorExplanations.a: Zone 2 intervals are added in Stage 2, once the client tolerates steady Zone 1 work for about 30 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Zone 3 near-maximal intervals belong to Stage 3 for well-conditioned clients, not a deconditioned start.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping straight to near-maximal bouts skips the Zone 2 progression and exceeds a beginner's tolerance.

prompt: A client moves from Phase 1 into the strength level (Phases 2–4). Which flexibility approach does NASM pair with this level?

options.text: Self-myofascial release followed by active-isolated stretching
Self-myofascial release followed by static stretching
Self-myofascial release followed by dynamic, full-range stretching
Ballistic bouncing stretches held briefly at end range

explanation: NASM's flexibility continuum is corrective (SMR plus static stretching) in stabilization, active (SMR plus active-isolated stretching with short 1–2 s holds) in strength, and functional (SMR plus dynamic stretching) in power.

distractorExplanations.b: SMR plus static stretching is corrective flexibility, used in the stabilization level.
distractorExplanations.c: SMR plus dynamic stretching is functional flexibility, used in the power level (Phase 5).
distractorExplanations.d: Ballistic stretching uses momentum at end range and is not part of NASM's flexibility continuum for most clients.

prompt: In the cumulative injury cycle, tissue trauma leads to inflammation. Which step comes next, before adhesions form?

options.text: Altered neuromuscular control
Muscle imbalance
Collagen remodeling
Muscle spasm

explanation: The cumulative injury cycle runs: tissue trauma, inflammation, muscle spasm, adhesions, altered neuromuscular control, muscle imbalance, then more trauma. Self-myofascial release and stretching aim to break the cycle at the spasm and adhesion stages.

distractorExplanations.a: Altered neuromuscular control follows adhesions; it is a later step, not the one right after inflammation.
distractorExplanations.b: Muscle imbalance is the final step that feeds back into new tissue trauma, closing the cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Collagen remodeling along lines of stress (Davis's law) shapes adhesions but is not the named step after inflammation.

prompt: For a client whose low back arches in the overhead squat, the trainer has foam-rolled and statically stretched the hip flexors. What is the next step of the corrective exercise continuum?

options.text: Integrate with a total-body pattern such as a ball wall squat
Activate the gluteus maximus with an isolated floor bridge
Inhibit the gluteus maximus with a foam roller
Lengthen the hamstrings with a static stretch next

explanation: NASM's corrective exercise continuum is inhibit (SMR), lengthen (static or neuromuscular stretching), activate (isolated strengthening of underactive muscles), then integrate (total-body movement). After the hip flexors are inhibited and lengthened, the glutes and core are activated.

distractorExplanations.a: Integration is the final step, after the underactive muscle has been activated in isolation.
distractorExplanations.c: Inhibition is for overactive tissue; the gluteus maximus is underactive here and needs activation.
distractorExplanations.d: The hamstrings are not the overactive muscles in low back arching, and lengthening is the step just done.

prompt: A Phase 1 program lists a tempo of 4/2/1 for a dumbbell squat. How should the client perform each rep?

options.text: 4 s lowering, 2 s pause at the bottom, 1 s rising
4 s rising, 2 s pause at the top, 1 s lowering
4 reps per set, 2 sets, and 1 minute of rest
1 s lowering, 2 s pause at the bottom, 4 s rising

explanation: NASM writes tempo as eccentric/isometric/concentric. In a 4/2/1 squat the client lowers for 4 seconds, holds the bottom for 2 seconds and stands up in 1 second, increasing time under tension and joint control in Phase 1.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the phases; NASM tempo lists the eccentric (lowering) phase first, then isometric, then concentric.
distractorExplanations.c: Tempo numbers describe seconds per phase of one rep, not reps, sets or rest periods.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads the numbers backward; the first number (4) is the eccentric phase, so the lowering is slow.

prompt: A client trains Monday in Phase 2, Wednesday in Phase 3, and Friday in Phase 4, repeating the cycle each week. Which periodization model is this?

options.text: Linear (classic) periodization
Reverse linear periodization
Block periodization with one focus per month
Undulating (nonlinear) periodization

explanation: Undulating periodization varies acute variables, here whole OPT phases, within the week, which suits clients with several goals. Linear periodization progresses through phases in sequential blocks over several weeks.

distractorExplanations.a: Linear periodization moves through phases in sequential blocks of weeks, not a different phase each day.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverse linear periodization moves from heavy to lighter loads across blocks, not rotating within a week.
distractorExplanations.c: Block periodization concentrates on one quality per block of weeks rather than rotating qualities each session.

prompt: A client wants a time-efficient circuit that alternates an upper-body exercise with a lower-body exercise to keep blood circulating. Which resistance-training system fits?

options.text: Pyramid (light-to-heavy) system
Peripheral heart action system
Drop-set (strip-set) system
Split-routine (body-part) system

explanation: Peripheral heart action is a circuit variation that alternates upper- and lower-body exercises so blood is shunted between regions, keeping heart rate elevated. NASM uses PHA for general fitness and fat-loss goals across OPT phases.

distractorExplanations.a: The pyramid system raises or lowers load across sets of one exercise; it does not alternate body regions.
distractorExplanations.c: Drop sets cut the load after failure on one exercise to extend the set rather than alternating regions.
distractorExplanations.d: Split routines train different body parts on different days rather than alternating them within a circuit.

prompt: Which plyometric drill is most appropriate as a client's first exposure in the stabilization level?

options.text: Box jump-up with a 3–5 second stabilized landing
Repeated tuck jumps performed as fast as possible
Depth jumps from a high box into a rebound jump
Single-leg power step-ups with explosive drive

explanation: Stabilization-level plyometrics (box jump-up, squat jump or multiplanar jump with stabilization) hold the landing for 3–5 seconds so the client learns safe deceleration. Repeated jumps come in the strength level and fast reactive drills in power.

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated tuck jumps are a strength-level drill with continuous reactive jumping, too advanced for a first exposure.
distractorExplanations.c: Depth jumps impose very high landing forces and belong to the power level for well-trained clients.
distractorExplanations.d: Explosive single-leg drills belong to the power level, after stabilization and strength are built.

prompt: A client with medically cleared, controlled hypertension begins resistance training. Which modification is most appropriate?

options.text: Use heavy 1–3 rep sets so the heart gets stronger more quickly
Favor head-down positions to improve blood return
Skip the cool-down to keep the session shorter
Use circuits, avoid breath-holding, and limit isometric holds

explanation: For clients with hypertension, NASM recommends circuit or PHA-style training with moderate loads, normal breathing (no Valsalva), avoiding heavy gripping and head-below-heart positions, and a longer cool-down, all with physician clearance.

distractorExplanations.a: Maximal loads spike blood pressure; controlled hypertension calls for moderate loads, not heavy singles.
distractorExplanations.b: Positions with the head below the heart raise blood pressure and should be avoided with hypertension.
distractorExplanations.c: An extended, gradual cool-down is advised so blood pressure does not drop abruptly after exercise.

prompt: A client in her second trimester with physician clearance wants to keep training. Which modification is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop resistance training until after delivery
Avoid lying flat on the back for prolonged periods
Add heavy core flexion such as weighted crunches
Push intensity close to maximal to offset weight gain

explanation: After the first trimester, prolonged supine positions can compress the vena cava and reduce blood return, so exercises move to inclined, seated or standing positions. Moderate, RPE-guided training continues with medical clearance.

distractorExplanations.a: Moderate resistance training is safe for most cleared pregnant clients; it does not need to stop.
distractorExplanations.c: Heavy spinal flexion strains the stretched abdominal wall and is avoided as pregnancy progresses.
distractorExplanations.d: Near-maximal efforts are not recommended; moderate intensity guided by RPE and the talk test is used.

prompt: When coaching a goblet squat, where should the client's knees track?

options.text: In line with the second and third toes
Pressed inward toward each other for stability
Pushed far outside the little toes
Kept behind the heels throughout the movement

explanation: The knees should track over the second and third toes so the hip, knee and ankle stay aligned. Inward drift (valgus) or forced outward flare changes joint loading, and some forward knee travel over the feet is normal.

distractorExplanations.b: Knees moving inward is a valgus compensation that stresses the knee, not a stable position.
distractorExplanations.c: Forcing the knees well outside the feet shifts load poorly; they should follow the line of the toes.
distractorExplanations.d: Knees cannot stay behind the heels in a squat; some forward knee travel over the feet is normal.

prompt: A client performs lat pulldowns by pulling the bar behind the neck. What is the best coaching correction?

options.text: Keep pulling behind the neck but switch to a lighter load
Lean back about 45 degrees and pull to the navel
Use a narrower grip and pull behind the neck faster
Pull the bar to the upper chest with a neutral spine

explanation: Behind-the-neck pulldowns force the shoulder into extreme abduction and external rotation and push the head forward, raising impingement and neck strain risk. Pulling to the upper chest with a neutral spine trains the lats safely.

distractorExplanations.a: A lighter load still places the shoulder in end-range abduction and external rotation behind the neck.
distractorExplanations.b: A big lean turns the move into a row, and pulling to the navel strays from the pulldown pattern.
distractorExplanations.c: Speeding up a behind-the-neck pull adds momentum and does not remove the risky shoulder position.

prompt: Over three weeks, a client's morning resting heart rate rises, sleep worsens, and lifts get weaker despite full effort. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Overtraining from too much stress and too little recovery
Normal progressive overload that will pass within a few days
A need to add training volume to break the plateau
Detraining caused by too few weekly sessions

explanation: A rising resting heart rate, disturbed sleep, low mood and falling performance despite effort are classic signs of overtraining or nonfunctional overreaching. The fix is reduced volume or intensity, more recovery and a review of total life stress.

distractorExplanations.b: Progressive overload should improve performance; a multi-week decline with poor sleep signals excess stress.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding volume deepens the problem; the response is to reduce load, prioritize sleep and review stressors.
distractorExplanations.d: Detraining comes from too little stimulus and does not raise resting heart rate or disturb sleep.

prompt: A client's lunch contains 30 g of protein, 50 g of carbohydrate, and 20 g of fat. About how many calories does it provide?

options.text: 400 kcal
460 kcal
500 kcal
650 kcal

explanation: Protein and carbohydrate provide about 4 kcal/g and fat about 9 kcal/g: (30 × 4) + (50 × 4) + (20 × 9) = 120 + 200 + 180 = 500 kcal.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts fat at 4 kcal/g like protein and carbohydrate; fat provides about 9 kcal/g.
distractorExplanations.b: Counts fat at 7 kcal/g, which is the value for alcohol; fat provides about 9 kcal/g.
distractorExplanations.d: Counts protein at 9 kcal/g; protein provides about 4 kcal/g, the same as carbohydrate.

prompt: A client wants to lose weight as fast as possible. What rate of loss is generally recommended as safe and sustainable?

options.text: About 0.1 kg (0.25 lb) per week
About 0.5–1 kg (1–2 lb) per week
About 2–3 kg (4–6 lb) per week
About 4–5 kg (9–11 lb) per week

explanation: Most guidelines advise about 1–2 lb (0.5–1 kg) per week, typically from a daily deficit of roughly 500–1,000 kcal. Faster loss increases muscle loss, fatigue and rebound risk, although early water loss can briefly exceed this.

distractorExplanations.a: Such a slow rate is safe but well below the 1–2 lb per week that guidelines support for most adults.
distractorExplanations.c: Sustained losses of 4–6 lb per week need an aggressive deficit that costs muscle and adherence.
distractorExplanations.d: Losing 9–11 lb a week would need an extreme deficit and is not safe without medical supervision.

prompt: A client loses 2 lb of body weight during a hot training session. Following common rehydration guidance, about how much fluid should they drink afterward?
explanation: Common guidance is to drink about 16–24 oz (0.5–0.7 L) of fluid for every pound lost during exercise. Losing 2 lb means about 32–48 oz, ideally with some sodium if sweat losses were large.

distractorExplanations.a: 8–12 oz would not replace even one pound of loss; guidance is 16–24 oz per pound lost.
distractorExplanations.b: 16–24 oz is the amount per pound; with 2 lb lost the client needs double, about 32–48 oz.
distractorExplanations.d: Far more than needed; 2 lb × 16–24 oz gives about 32–48 oz, and overdrinking risks hyponatremia.

prompt: The Dietary Reference Intakes set adequate fiber at about 14 g per 1,000 kcal. About how much fiber does a client eating 2,000 kcal per day need?
explanation: Fiber adequacy is about 14 g per 1,000 kcal, so 2,000 kcal × 14 g ÷ 1,000 = 28 g per day. Most adults fall well short, so trainers can encourage whole grains, legumes, fruits and vegetables within general guidelines.

distractorExplanations.a: 14 g is the amount per 1,000 kcal; a 2,000 kcal diet doubles it to about 28 g.
distractorExplanations.b: 20 g falls short of the target; it is closer to typical intake, while 2 × 14 g = 28 g.
distractorExplanations.d: 40 g exceeds the target for 2,000 kcal; it matches roughly 2,850 kcal at 14 g per 1,000.

prompt: A client asks which foods supply the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA. Which choice is best?

options.text: Flaxseed oil
Extra-virgin olive oil and avocado
Coconut oil
Fatty fish such as salmon

explanation: EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 fatty acids found mainly in fatty fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel. Plant sources such as flax provide ALA, which the body converts to EPA and DHA only in small amounts.

distractorExplanations.a: Flax supplies ALA, a plant omega-3 that the body converts to EPA and DHA only in small amounts.
distractorExplanations.b: Olive oil and avocado are rich in monounsaturated fat (oleic acid), not the long-chain omega-3s EPA and DHA.
distractorExplanations.c: Coconut oil is mostly saturated fat and provides essentially no EPA or DHA.

prompt: A client trains at 6 p.m. and asks what to eat around 3 p.m. Which general guideline best fits?

options.text: A carbohydrate-rich meal with moderate protein, lower in fat and fiber
A high-fat, high-fiber meal to keep energy levels steady during training
Skip eating, since fasted training maximizes fat loss
A protein shake with no carbohydrate to avoid insulin

explanation: A meal 2–4 hours before training should emphasize carbohydrate to top up glycogen, include moderate protein, and keep fat and fiber modest so it digests comfortably. This is general guidance, not an individualized meal plan.

distractorExplanations.b: Fat and fiber slow digestion and can cause GI discomfort when eaten close to a session.
distractorExplanations.c: Fasted training does not improve fat loss when calories are matched and can reduce session quality.
distractorExplanations.d: Carbohydrate before training tops up glycogen; avoiding insulin is not a pre-workout priority.

prompt: A client says, 'I know I should exercise, and I'm thinking about starting sometime in the next few months.' Which stage of change is this?

options.text: Precontemplation
Preparation
Action
Contemplation

explanation: In the transtheoretical model, contemplation means the person sees the need to change and intends to act within about six months but has not committed. Trainers help by weighing pros and cons and building confidence.

distractorExplanations.a: Precontemplation means the person is not yet considering change within the next six months.
distractorExplanations.b: Preparation means the person plans to act within the next month and is already taking small steps.
distractorExplanations.c: Action means the person has been exercising regularly, but for less than six months.

prompt: A trainer wants to build a hesitant client's self-efficacy for exercise. Which source of self-efficacy is generally the most powerful?

options.text: Mastery experiences of succeeding at tasks
Verbal persuasion and encouragement from the trainer
Watching others similar to them succeed
Physiological arousal felt before a workout

explanation: Bandura identified mastery (performance) experiences as the strongest source of self-efficacy. Programming early, achievable wins and progressing gradually lets clients prove to themselves that they can succeed.

distractorExplanations.b: Encouragement helps, but it is weaker than the client's own direct experience of success.
distractorExplanations.c: Vicarious experience is a meaningful source, but secondary to personal mastery.
distractorExplanations.d: Physiological and emotional states influence confidence but are the least direct source.

prompt: A client says early workouts are hard because of work travel. The trainer replies, 'So travel makes your morning routine tough to keep.' Which communication skill is this?

options.text: Closed-ended questioning
Giving directive advice
Positive reinforcement
Reflective listening

explanation: Reflective listening restates or paraphrases what the client said so they feel heard and can correct or expand on it. It builds rapport and is a core skill alongside open-ended questions in client-centered coaching.

distractorExplanations.a: No question is asked; a closed-ended question would invite a yes/no or one-word answer.
distractorExplanations.b: The trainer offers no instruction or solution; the statement mirrors the client's meaning.
distractorExplanations.c: Reinforcement praises a desired behavior; this reply restates the client's concern instead.

prompt: A client has exercised consistently for two months but expects a busy holiday season. Which strategy best supports adherence?

options.text: Pause all training until the schedule settles down
Raise session frequency now to bank a fitness buffer first
Rely on willpower to keep the full routine unchanged
Plan for high-risk situations with a scaled-back routine

explanation: Relapse prevention identifies high-risk situations in advance and plans coping strategies, such as shorter home workouts during holidays, so a lapse does not become a full relapse. Treating a missed session as a slip, not failure, also helps.

distractorExplanations.a: Stopping completely makes restarting harder; a planned minimum routine keeps the habit alive.
distractorExplanations.b: Extra sessions before a busy period add fatigue and do not prevent lapses when time runs out.
distractorExplanations.c: Willpower alone tends to fail under stress; planning for barriers is more effective.

prompt: During a consultation, which statement presents a benefit rather than a feature of personal training?

options.text: Each session lasts 60 minutes in a private studio
I hold a NASM-CPT and a current CPR/AED card
Packages include a quarterly fitness reassessment session
You'll be able to play with your kids without back pain

explanation: Features describe the service (session length, credentials, assessments); benefits describe the outcome the client cares about, such as playing with their kids comfortably. Linking features to personal benefits keeps a consultation client-centered.

distractorExplanations.a: Session length and location describe a feature of the service, not what the client gains.
distractorExplanations.b: Credentials are a feature that builds trust; a benefit links the service to the client's goal.
distractorExplanations.c: A reassessment is a service feature; the benefit would be the outcome it delivers to the client.

prompt: A trainer averages 25 sessions per week at $60 each and works 48 weeks per year. What is the trainer's gross annual session revenue?
explanation: Weekly revenue = 25 sessions × $60 = $1,500. Annual revenue = $1,500 × 48 weeks = $72,000 gross, before taxes, facility fees, insurance and continuing-education costs.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 40 working weeks; the trainer works 48, so $1,500 × 48 = $72,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses all 52 weeks; with 48 working weeks, $1,500 × 48 = $72,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes 30 sessions per week; 25 sessions × $60 = $1,500 weekly, then × 48 = $72,000.

prompt: A trainer notices a client has lost a lot of weight quickly, skips meals, and talks about 'burning off' everything she eats. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Write her a higher-calorie meal plan to restore weight
Increase her cardio so she feels she can eat more
Diagnose an eating disorder and tell her family
Voice concern privately and refer to a qualified professional

explanation: Signs of disordered eating call for a private, nonjudgmental conversation and referral to a physician, registered dietitian or mental health professional. Trainers do not diagnose or treat eating disorders and should not add exercise that reinforces them.

distractorExplanations.a: Designing a therapeutic meal plan for a suspected eating disorder is outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding exercise reinforces compensatory behavior and can worsen a suspected eating disorder.
distractorExplanations.c: Trainers cannot diagnose, and telling family without consent breaches confidentiality.

prompt: Alongside continuing education units, which credential must a NASM Certified Personal Trainer keep current to recertify?

options.text: A state personal trainer license from the local licensing board
A registered dietitian credential for nutrition advice
A first-aid card completed entirely online
Adult CPR and AED certification with a hands-on skills check

explanation: NASM requires CPTs to recertify every two years by earning continuing education units and holding a current adult CPR and AED certification that includes a hands-on skills component; online-only cards are not accepted.

distractorExplanations.a: Most US states do not license personal trainers; NASM recertification relies on CEUs plus CPR/AED.
distractorExplanations.b: Trainers do not need an RD credential; they stay within general nutrition guidance instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Online courses without a hands-on skills check do not meet NASM's CPR/AED requirement.

prompt: A client plans to take high-dose vitamins 'because extra just gets flushed out.' Which vitamins are most likely to build up to toxic levels?

options.text: Water-soluble vitamin C and thiamin
Electrolyte minerals sodium and potassium
Carotenoids such as lycopene and lutein
Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K

explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) are stored in the liver and fatty tissue, so megadoses can accumulate to toxic levels. Water-soluble vitamins are mostly excreted, though some, such as B6, can still cause harm at very high doses. Dosing questions go to a clinician.

distractorExplanations.a: Vitamin C and thiamin are water-soluble; excess is mostly excreted, so toxicity is less likely.
distractorExplanations.b: These are minerals, not vitamins, and the kidneys regulate them under normal intake.
distractorExplanations.c: Carotenoids from food are not stored to toxic levels; high-dose preformed vitamin A is the concern.
